items.e: A wooden plank that is placed over the mouth of an old oven and impurity is inside of or on top of [the oven], everything is impure and the oven is impure, and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri renders the oven pure * . [If] one of its ends was placed over the mouth of a new oven, and the other end was placed over the mouth of an old oven, or if there were two old [ovens], one on this side and one on that side, and a new oven in the middle, Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri renders the oven pure * . A wooden plank that is placed over the mouth of an oven and it is sealed with a tightly fitting lid under it or on top of it, everything is impure, and that which is directly [above] the airspace of the oven is pure. [If] impurity [is directly above] the airspace of the oven, that which is directly [above the impurity], up until the firmament, is impure.

Netting that is placed over the mouth of [a new] oven and it projected out even the smallest amount, and it has an edge [the height of] of a handbreadth: [If] impurity is under it, vessels that are on top of it are pure (alt., "impure" (GR"A)). [If] impurity is is on top of it, vessels that are under it are pure (alt., "impure" (GR"A)). And if it was flat, behold, it is like a wooden board and it requires a handbreadth's opening. And Rabbi Eliezer agrees that with regard to a window-projection * , that if it was made made [for that purpose] from the beginning, it does bring in impurity.

The shoe (i.e., the metal base) of a cradle, some of which [protrudes] from the plasterwork [which coats the ceiling]: Its measure is a handbreadth's opening. If the house opened up on its own, its measure is the size of a fist. If even the smallest amount of plaster was visible under it: If it was from the upper half of the plasterwork, then whether it possesses the [minimum] measure, or whether it does not possess the minimum measure, the house is pure. If it was from the lower half of the plasterwork, then if it possesses the [minimum] measure, the house is impure, and if not, its [impurity] is reckoned in the same way that [impurity due to contact with] a corpse is reckoned (Mishnah Oholot 12:4).

A bed frame upholstered with tufts [of material], a baby [who is placed on frame] is impure with seven-day impurity. [If] it was girded with ropes, a baby is impure with evening-impurity * . A plank of reeds that was girded with ropes and covered with plaster, [and] a loaf of bread that was soaked in fruit juices is placed on top of it -- behold, it brings in and protects against [impurity]. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri says, [as to] all pure cakes, they do not bring in impurity, except for fig-cakes, for they sit (i.e., are stored) in pits underneath [peoples' homes].

A camel that is standing in the airspace [of a source of impurity]: [If] impurity is beneath it, vessels that are on top of it (lit., "on its back") are pure. [If] impurity is on top of it, vessels that are beneath it are pure. [If the camel] was kneeling down, [and] impurity is below it, that which is directly [below] it, until the depths [of the earth], is impure. [If] impurity is on top of it, that which is directly [above] it, until the firmament, is impure. [If] impurity is under its leg or on top of its leg and it kneels down, the impurity breaks forth and ascends, breaks forth and descends. [If] he placed a wooden board above it, [and] impurity is on one side, vessels that are on the other side are impure.

Roof-beams of the house and the attic that are in a line opposite the lower [beams] (see Mishnah Oholot 12:5): [If] impurity is beneath [the lower beams], then [the area below them] is impure; between [the upper and lower beams], between them is impure, but on top of them is pure. [If impurity] is on top of them, [then the area] directly above it up to the firmament is impure, and below them is pure. When do these words apply? When there is a handbreadth's opening between them, [but] if there is not a handbreadth's opening between them, impurity breaks forth and ascends, breaks forth and descends.

A seah -measure that was laying on its side in the airspace [of a source of impurity] does not bring in impurity underneath its entire [expanse] unless its circumference is four and a half handbreadths (alt., "four handbreadths" (GR"A)). If it was raised half a handbreadth [off the ground], [it does not bring in impurity] unless its circumference is three handbreadths. A column (i.e., which was narrow at top and bottom but bulged in the middle) that was taken into the airspace [of a source of impurity] does not bring in impurity under its side (i.e., under the widest expanse of its bulge) unless its circumference is twenty-four handbreadths. Rabbi Yosei says, twenty-five, for the earth does not absorb (lit., "eat") a handbreadth from them. And so too it says (Jer. 52:23), "And there were ninety-six pomegranates * facing outward," and then it says ( ibid. ), "all the pomegranates around the meshwork were one hundred." How is it possible to say "around the meshwork were one hundred" when, behold, it has already said "ninety-six," and how is it possible to say "ninety-six" when it has already said "one hundred"? It was said, from this point forward, four [of the pomegranates] shall be absorbed into the wall, and ninety-six shall be seen from the outside, and its courtyard shall be adjudged like the sloping sides of a tent.

An olive-bulk of a corpse that is stuck in the threshold: Rabbi Eliezer renders the house impure and Rabbi Yehoshua renders it pure (Mishnah Oholot 12:8). [If] it was placed under the threshold, it is adjudged half-and-half for [purposes of] impurity * , the words of Rabbi Ya'akov. Said Rabbi Shimon, Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua did not disagree about [an olive-bulk] placed under the threshold, that the house is pure. About what did they disagree? About that which is stuck in the threshold, for Rabbi Eliezer renders the house impure and Rabbi Yehoshua renders it pure. [If] it was stuck in the lintel, the house is impure, and Rabbi Yehoshua (alt., "Rabbi Yosei"; MS Vienna, GR"A) renders it pure, unless it is pushed out by a handbreadth's opening (i.e., the corpse-matter itself forms a tent).

[If there are] two door-projections ( zizin ) * , this one on top of that one, and impurity is in the wall that is between them: If even the smallest amount could be seen inside one of them, it is impure, and its fellow is pure, and if not, it is adjudged half-and-half (i.e., the door-projection closest to the impurity is deemed impure, and the other is pure).

Funeral processions that were passing through a public thoroughfare: One's own tent joins together with the tent of the corpse to defile the house, the words of Rabbi Eliezer. And Rabbi Yehoshua says, we do not raise up that which is lower down (i.e., the funeral procession) for [the purpose of] joining tent with tent.

An opening that was made for the purpose of [it serving as] a light hole, its [minimum] measure [to bring impurity to the other side of the opening] is the size of a drill-hole. [If] they sealed up [a larger opening (e.g., a doorway)] for the purpose of [it serving as] a light hole, its measure is a handbreadth's opening. Two windows, this one inside that one: [If] the outer one is made into a light hole, its measure is the size of a drill-hole.

[If] the shutter of a window-pane was removed, its measure is the size of a fist. And these are the "remains of a light hole" (Mishnah Oholot 13:1): A window that was sealed but there was not enough plaster to complete [the job], or where [the laborer's] fellows * called him or it became dark on the night of Shabbat [before the job was completed]. And these are [the minimum measures for impurity to be conveyed through] the remains of a light hole: The height of two fingerbreadths and the width of a thumb-breadth.

A window that is between two houses (i.e., which share a common wall): Its measure is a handbreadth's opening. [If] he concealed the outer one, even if he did not intend it, its measure is the size of a drill-hole. [If] the roof was placed [at the height of] the middle of the window, the measure of the lower part [is a handbreadth's-opening, and of the upper part that of drill-hole]. * And what are the "lattices" and the "gratings" (**רפפות**, MS Vienna) (i.e., whose holes join to form an opening the size of a drill-hole (Mishnah Oholot 13:1))? These (i.e., lattices) are those of storehouses, and those (i.e., gratings) are those of house-annexes. Rabbi Shimon ben Gamaliel says, windows that are in walled cities -- their measure is a handbreadth's opening, for they are only made for fortification, [for] they cause the wind to blow over them * .

Rabbi Yehuda says concerning these * , three measurements in the name of Rabbi Akiva: One who makes [an opening in the wall] for conversation * , or for guarding, or for enjoying the view (lit., "feeding his eyes"), [impurity is conveyed through] even the smallest size. For bringing in vessels and taking out vessels, for [human] use, and for a lamp, its measure is a handbreadth's opening. For a [weaver's] reed (**לקנה**) but not for his stave * -- Beit Shammai say, [an opening] of its full length, and Beit Hillel say, a handbreadth's opening.

Rabbi Yehuda says, even the thigh-bone of Og reduces the handbreadth['s opening], and so too would Rabbi Yehuda say, * less than an olive's-bulk of flesh reduces [the minimum opening for impurity] caused by a quarter-kav of bones (Mishnah Oholot 13:5). Less than a barleycorn's-bulk of bone reduces [the minimum opening for impurity] caused by an olive's-bulk of flesh. And an olive's-bulk from a carcass [of an animal], or a lentil's-bulk from a sheretz, do not reduce it, but Rabbi Yehuda says they do reduce it. This is the general rule: Said Rebbi, any impurity that is not from a [human] corpse, or that is from a corpse but does not join together with the same [type of] impurity, behold, that reduces.

Grasses that one detached [from the earth] and placed in a window, or that grew on their own [in the window]; or a bird that dwells in the window; or scraps of fabric that were less than three-by-three [fingerbreadths]; or a limb or flesh that are dangling from a domesticated animal or a animal or birds; or an idolator or a domesticated animal or an eight-year-old or an earthenware vessel or food or drink or a Torah scroll or salt -- behold, all of these reduce [the handbreadth's opening]. But snow and hail and frost and ice and water do not reduce.

A projection that is on top of the remains of a light hole * : Its measure is the height of two fingerbreadths by the width of a thumb-breadth. And that which is on top of [an opening] the size of drill-hole: [Its measure is] even the smallest size. Rabbi Yosei says, its full size, and [in regards to] a projection that is on top of the entrance, its measure is even the smallest size. [If] they sealed it off, its measure is a handbreadth's opening. [If] they opened it up [again], its measure is even the smallest size.

Two projections -- this one on top of that one -- and the entrance is underneath them -- [the measure of] the lower one * is even the smallest size, and [with respect to] the higher one, even if it is a distance of three courses of stones which is twelve handbreadths, its measure is a handbreadth's opening. [If the upper one] concealed or overlapped the lower one, its measure is even the smallest size.

Two entrances -- this one on top of that one -- and the projection is higher than them: [The measure of impurity] for the upper one is even the smallest size, and for the lower one, even if it is a distance of three courses of stones which is twelve handbreadths, its measure is a handbreadth's opening. [If] the upper [entrance] was sealed off or [if] it overlapped the lower one by a handbreadth on one side and a handbreadth on the other side, its measure is even the smallest size. When do we say even the smallest size [of a projection * ] that juts out [from the wall brings impurity], but a gavlit [does not bring impurity] unless it has a handbreadth's opening? And what is a " gavlit " (Mishnah Oholot 14:1)? Any [balcony] that "suckles" * [from the wall] on one side and on the other side, and left alone (i.e., without support) from the middle. Rabbi Yosei b'Rabbi Yehuda says, the crowns and the engravings (**פיתוחין**) and the mouldings bring in impurity. Rebbi says, the stringency concerning the [weaver's] reed is greater than that of the projection, for the [weaver's] reed is carried around, and the projection is not carried around.

A projection that juts out from a wall, and there is a handbreadth's opening in it: [If] impurity is under them, and vessels are in the wall and above them [separated from the projection] by the width of a garlic peel, they are pure. [If] impurity is in the wall, and vessels are under them and above them [separated from the projection] by the width of a garlic peel, they are pure.

Marble slabs divided [into two], and placed one on top of the other: [If] impurity is under one of them, and even if they are raised up from the ground by a cubit, impurity breaks forth and ascends, breaks forth and descends. Slabs touching one another, or tables touching one another: They are reckoned [for purposes of impurity] in the same way that [contact with] a corpse is reckoned.

A slab [placed] at the side of a table leg, and impurity is under the slab: One who touches either the slab or the table is impure with seven-day impurity. [If] impurity is under the table: One who touches the table is impure with seven-day impurity, and [one who touches] the slab is impure with evening-impurity. A tent directly above the "square" [of the table (see Mishnah Oholot 15:2)] * is impure; that which is not directly above the "square" is pure. Rabbi Menachem b'Rabbi Yosei says, either this way or that way, they are impure, because they are adjudged like the "corner of the slab" (see ibid.).

Jars that are lying [on their side] in the open, [and] the surrounding rim of this one is on the side of the airspace of the surrounding rim * of that one, and the surrounding rim of that one is on top of the side of that this one, one handbreadth above the ground, and the surrounding rims have a handbreadth's opening [between them]: [If] impurity is below them, that which is above them is impure. On top of them, that which is on top of them and below them is impure and that which is inside them is pure. [If] they are raised one handbreadth off the ground, and their surrounding rims do not have a handbreadth's opening [between them], and impurity is under one of them, that which is below them or above them is impure. Above it, that which is above it is impure, and that which is below it is impure, and that which is inside it is pure. When do these words apply? With regard to pure [jars], but if they were impure, and they were raised off the ground by a handbreadth, [and] impurity is under one of them, [the area] under all of them is impure.

A house that was partitioned off by planks or by curtains from the sides or from the roof beams (Mishnah Oholot 15:4), and impurity is in the wall * : Vessels that are in the partition are impure, and those that are in the back side of the wall * or in the upper side of the plasterwork [which coats the ceiling] are adjudged half-and-half. [If] there are four handbreadths there, the [protective capacity of the] wall is nullified. Rebbi says, the one who says "a handbreadth" may say (alt., "may not say" (GR"A)) "four [handbreadths]," [and] the one who says "four [handbreadths]" may not say "a handbreadth." [If] they partitioned it off from its ground (i.e., from the floor of the house), and impurity is in the partition, vessels that are in the house are impure. [If] impurity is in the house, vessels that are in the partition are pure. If the partition has in their place (i.e., where the vessels are located) [a space of] a handbreadth by a handbreadth by a handbreadth high, it is pure, and if not, they are impure, and those which are in the ground are impure. [If] impurity is in the ground, vessels that are in the partition are pure and those which are in the house are impure.

A house that is filled with straw, and there is not (alt., "there is" (GR"A)) the space of a handbreadth between [the straw] and the roofbeams, and impurity is from the inside [of the house], anything that is directly [above or below] the exit-point of the impurity in the entire open space [of the exit] is impure, and [if impurity is] in the portico, [the impurity spreads] only opposite the impurity from the roofbeams and outside. And Rabbi Yosei says, straw that one does not intend to clear out in the future, behold, it is like dirt; and dirt that one does intend to clear out in the future, behold, it is like straw.

A mound of pebbles, and so too a heap of produce, and impurity is within it: Impurity breaks forth and ascends, breaks forth and descends, and if in the place of the impurity [there is a space of] a handbreadth by a handbreadth by a handbreadth high, behold, it is [adjudged to be] like a sealed grave, and it defiles all its surroundings. And what is the "courtyard of the grave" (Mishnah Oholot 15:8)? That is the marked space into which the caverns open. If it possesses the minimum measure, that which enters into it is impure * . When do these words apply? At a time that it is not open to the air, but at a time that it is open to the air, even if it does not cleave to the lintel * by even the smallest amount, it is pure, as long as it does not touch the lintel.

A mound of pebbles that they made into a covering-stone for a grave: One who approaches it within four handbreadths is impure, the words of Rabbi Yehuda. [ * And the Sages say, only the one who lays down (alt., "arranges" (GR"A)) the inner [layer of pebbles] for the needs of the grave is impure. Rebbi says, the words of Rabbi Yehuda are preferable] when one does not intend to level it * , and the words of the Sages are preferable when one does intend to level it.

[An earthenware] cask that is filled with [pure] liquids and has a tightly fitting lid, and is made to serve as the covering-stone for a grave (Mishnah Oholot 15:9): Said Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon, concerning this, Beit Shammai render impure and Beit Hillel render pure. Said Beit Shammai to Beit Hillel: "Which more commonly contracts impurity, a person or liquids?" They said to them, "Liquids." They said to them, "And thus, if a person, for whom contracting impurity is not common, is defiled as soon as he touches it, then as to the liquids that are inside it, does it not follow that they would [also] be defiled?" Beit Hillel said to them, "Do you not concede that with regard to a pure [person] who swallowed a [pure] ring and entered the tent of a corpse, that even though [the person] is defiled with seven-day impurity, the ring is pure?" Beit Shammai said to them, "No. If you are speaking of a ring, which is not defiled through carriage by a zav, what would you say regarding liquids, which are defiled through carriage by a zav?" Beit Hillel said to them, "We are applying the logic of seven-day impurity from [another case of] seven-day impurity, and you are applying the logic of seven-day impurity from [a case of] evening-impurity. Is it not better to apply the logic of seven-day impurity from [another case of] seven-day impurity, than to apply the logic of seven-day impurity from [a case of] evening-impurity?" Another version: "A person who touches a corpse defiles vessels, and vessels that touch a corpse defile a person. A person who touches a corpse defiles earthenware vessels, but earthenware vessels that touch a corpse do not defile a person. And are these matters not deduced through a fortiori logic ( kal v'chomer )? Since if a person, who is defiled by a corpse and by that which touches a corpse, to [thereby] defile that which touches him, [but nonetheless] saves that which is inside of himself (e.g., the ring), [then as to] an earthenware vessel, which cannot be defiled by a corpse or by that which touches a corpse, to [thereby] defile that which touches it, does it not logically follow that [the earthenware vessel] would save that which is inside of itself (e.g., the liquids)?" Said Rabbi Shimon, they need not have exerted themselves to that extent. [Rather,] in a place that a person conveys impurity, from there liquids [also] convey impurity, [and] in a place that liquids are saved, from there a person is [also] saved. Where a person conveys impurity in an open place, so too liquids in an open place. Where liquids are saved inside, so too a person that they placed inside * [a container], and sealed him in with a tightly fitting lid, and made him into covering-stone for a grave, is pure.

All movable objects with the thickness of an ox-goad bring in impurity. Said Rabbi Tarfon: "I will bury ( ek'pach ) my sons if this halacha is not distorted ( m'kupechet )! I know not whence this ruling sprouted forth; rather, that the hearer heard it and erred. And it so happened with one who was passing by with an ox-goad on his shoulder, one side of which [passed] over a grave, and defiled him on account of 'one who overtents a corpse,' and the hearer heard it and erred (i.e., in deriving a ruling broader than these specific facts)." Said Rabbi Yehuda: "It so happened with one who was plowing, and shook the plow, and the skull of a corpse was found stuck in the plow, and it defiled him on account of 'one who overtents a corpse,' and the hearer heard it and erred." Said Rabbi Yehuda: "It so happened with one who was plowing, and shook the plow, and a complete skull was found stuck in the plow, and it defiled him on account of 'one who moves a corpse,' and the hearer heard it and erred."

An ox-goad that they placed on top of an animal, and one end is placed on top of a corpse and the other end is placed on top of a person, [or] one end is placed on top of a corpse and the other end is placed on top of vessels, is pure * . And [when they spoke of "a person"] they were only speaking of the person who carries [the ox-goad].

The mounds that are nearby, between one town and another town, or between roads: Whether they are new or old, they are impure, because women bury their stillborn fetuses there, and lepers bury their limbs there. New [mounds] that are far [from a town or road] are pure; old ones are impure, for I could say, "lest there was once a road or a town there." And what are these "mounds"? These are mounds of dirt that are on top of a cleft [in the earth]. One who erects a tent on top of part of [a mound] is impure and, needless to say, [one who pitches a tent] against all of it. Its dirt is impure on account of being "dirt of a mound." One who dug (חתר) dirt from it, and packed [more dirt] on it, it is not subject to the laws of "dirt of a mound." A mound that was impure and was purified, behold, it is pure, and one need not be concerned lest it revert to impurity.

It is the same whether one finds three corpses, or whether one finds three sepulchers, or whether one finds a sepulcher and a cleft grave and a hastily dug grave [at the same time], or whether one found ten and they do not have between four and eight cubits in between them: They all are subject to [the laws regarding the impurity of the] "surrounding earth," but they are subject to [the laws regarding the impurity of] a "graveyard site" (i.e., a cemetery) (see Mishnah Oholot 16:3), the words of Rabbi Shimon. And the Sages say, one looks at the middle ones as if they were not there, and the outer ones join together from four to eight cubits. [If] he found a [corpse's] head next to its legs, it is not subject to [the laws of] "surrounding earth," and it is not subject to [the laws of] a "graveyard site." The head of this one next to the body of that one, and the head of that one next to the body of this one: They are subject to [the laws of] "surrounding earth," but they are not subject to [the laws of] a "graveyard site." And that which is missing is subject neither to "surrounding earth" nor to a "graveyard site." And what does "missing" mean? Anything that would cause someone to die if it was removed when he was alive. [If] he found two [corpses] for the first time, and one [more] is known [to exist], they are subject to "surrounding earth," but they are not subject to a "graveyard site." It so happened with Rabbi Yeshevav, that he inspected and found two for the first time, and one was known. He made (i.e., designated) for them [an area of] "surrounding earth," [and] he made for them [an area of] a "graveyard site." When he came to the place of Rabbi Akiva, he said, "All your work was in vain. You would have had to inspect every known burial site in the Land of Israel (i.e., according to your logic). They only ruled regarding one who finds three [corpses] for the first time."

[If] one [grave] was found on one side of a public thoroughfare, and two [were found] on the other side, he inspects one side and the other side, and he leaves [a cubit] of the public thoroughfare [unchecked] (see Mishnah Oholot 16:4). Two on one side of a fence, and two on the other side of the fence: He inspects the area of the fence, for it is the [normal] way of a builder to inspect until he reaches the rock (i.e., the rocky substrata), or virgin soil. And what is "virgin soil"? Anything that does not have clods of fresh-broken ground, and does not have loose earth below it. [If] he inspected and reached water [below the surface], behold, that is virgin soil. [If] he inspected and found clay there, behold, that is like virgin soil. The one who inspects: Beit Shammai say, he checks two [cubits] and leaves one cubit [unchecked], and Beit Hillel say, he checks one cubit and leaves one cubit, the words of Rabbi Yaakov. And the Sages say, Beit Shammai say, he checks two [cubits] and leaves one cubit, and Beit Hillel say, he checks one cubit and leaves two.

One (i.e., a priest) who takes out dirt from an impure place may eat from his dema (i.e., terumah mixed with chullin). Rabbi Yehuda says, he piles this dirt on top of that dirt, but our Rabbis said, the dirt is pure. The one who inspects [the dirt to check for corpse matter] may eat from his dema . The students of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai asked him, "The inspector -- what should he eat?" He said to them, "He does not eat." They said to him, "You taught us that he does eat." He said to them, ""Well said. If I have forgotten an act that my own hands performed, and my own eyes witnessed, how much more so one that I have [only] heard with my ears!" And it was not that he did not know; rather, it was that he was trying to stimulate his students. For Rabbi Yehoshua would say, one who teaches and does not exercise [the minds of his students] is like one who sows and does not harvest. One who learns Torah and forgets it is like a woman who bears children and buries them. Rabbi Akiva says, "Review it; continuously review it."

It turns out that one can say that there are three graves: A grave that is discovered: They may remove it, [but once] it is removed, the area is impure, and forbidden to derive benefit from. A grave which endangers the public: They may remove it, [and once] it is removed, the area is pure and permitted to derive benefit from. A grave which is known: They may not remove it, [but] if they did remove it, they area is pure and permitted to derive benefit from. A field in which a grave was lost (i.e., its location was forgotten) is pure, [but] one who enters [the field] is impure. [If] he examined [the field] and found a grave inside it: One who enters [the field] is pure, for I could reason, "The grave that was lost is the grave that was found." [If] he examined and found three graves inside it: One who enters [the field] is pure, and one need not be concerned lest they are subject to [the laws of] a "graveyard site" (i.e., a cemetery) (see Mishnah Oholot 16:3). One who removes his grave (i.e., a grave on his property) to the public thoroughfare, and a person was walking there, he removes one bone [at a time], and everything is pure. One who dug out his grave inside his field, they say to him, "Collect it bone by bone, and everything is pure." It so happened with the brothers * Yehuda and Hillel, the sons of Rabban Gamaliel, that they were walking on the border of Oney, [and] they found a certain man who had dug up his grave inside of his field. They said to him, "Collect it bone by bone, and everything is pure."

One whose burial is unauthorized is not [considered] part of a "graveyard site" and is not subject to [the laws of] "the surrounding earth of the grave." Rabban Shimon ben Gamaliel says, a stillborn does not acquire a grave and is not subject to "surrounding earth," and one whose burial is unauthorized is subject to "surrounding earth." Rabbi Yehuda says, a pit into which stillborn are dropped is pure. Said Rabbi Yehuda, it so happened with a certain [Roman] tax collector in Rimon, that he dropped a stillborn into a pit, and a certain priest came with his front plate ( tzitz ) to determine what was dropped [into the pit], and that incident was brought before [the Sages] and they rendered it pure, because weasels and hyenas can be found there, and [it is presumed that] they would drag [the stillborn] from there (see Mishnah Oholot 18:8).

A grave that was sealed: [If] he opened it, it does not import impurity in any of the surrounding area. [If] he broke open its boards, and went back and sealed it, it imparts impurity on its surrounding area. [If] he made a breach in it, one breach of four handbreadths, whether above or below, it only imparts impurity opposite the breach. [If] he had opened one aperture to the north, and opened another aperture to the south, the south purifies the north.

One who plows a grave, behold, he must do (i.e., plow) one hundred cubits in each direction. One who plows on top of a grave, and so too one who plows on top of a coffin, even if he submerged it with chains or with stones, and even on top of holes that were twice a man's height, behold, that creates a beit haperas . One who plows up body of a dead person does not create a beit haperas ; rather one who only plows up the grave. And Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says, even the mound. Said Rabbi Yosei, when do these words apply? With regards to one who descends, but regarding one who ascends, he does not create a beit haperas .

The "three vetches" that they spoke about (Mishnah Oholot 17:1), are those that are placed there in their normal manner in a dry place, but not in a muddy place. And one who plows from a field full of scales (i.e., where refuse is deposited), or from a a sloping field, behold, he creates a beit haperas . The builder is pure and one who sows on top of it is pure. Rabbi Meir says, one who plows up a quarry [containing a deposit] of bones (Mishnah Oholot 17:3), behold, he creates a beit haperas .

Partners, and sharecroppers, and guardians [of orphans] do not create a beit haperas . One who plows inside his own [field] or inside that of his fellow: His [field] becomes a beit haperas , but that of his fellow does not become a beit haperas , but it ascends to the status of a peras .

The presumption is that [fields] in the Land of Israel are pure except for [those containing] heaps of stones. A field that they presumed to be a beit haperas : Even if it has an area [large enough to grow] four kors [of grain], even if it is adjacent to an impure place, and even if a pure field surrounds it on all sides, behold, it is presumed to possess the status of a peras .

Two fields of a beit haperas , this one on top of that one, and [the owners] had a partnership in rainwater: [If] there are are three handbreadths between the lower one and the upper one, both of them are impure. Rabbi Yosei says, even though there is no direct line between the entryway of the upper [field] and the upper house, it is pure.

A beit haperas that they purified: Behold, it is pure, but it must stand on the backs (i.e., the testimony) of two Torah scholars. Said Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages did not disagree about dirt that comes from a beit haperas that comes in with vegetables, that it is pure unless there is in one place [an amount of dirt] equivalent to the bulk of a packing-bag seal * . About what did they disagree? About dirt that comes in from the land of the nations with vegetables, that Rabbi Eliezer says, it combines, and the Sages say, it does not combine unless there is in one place [an amount of dirt] equivalent to the bulk of the seal of a letter.

One who brings chests or ovens or basins or earthenware vessels from outside the Land into the Land before they have been fired -- they are impure on account of the laws regarding the "land of the nations," but they are pure on account of the laws regarding earthenware vessels. Once they have been fired, they are impure on account of the laws regarding earthenware vessels, but they are pure on account of the laws regarding the "land of the nations." Consequently it is said, "Whenever [vessels are deemed] impure on account of [being produced in] the lands of the nations, they are pure on account of being earthenware vessels, and whenever [vessels are deemed] impure on account of being earthenware vessels, they are [deemed] pure on account of [being produced in] the lands of the [Gentile] nations."

One who brings dirt from an impure place and piles it up in a pure place, or from a pure place and piles it up in an impure place, it is impure. [If] he piled it up on top of a rock, even in an [im]pure place, it is pure. One who applies whitewash to a beit haperas in an impure place is impure, and in a pure place is pure. Rabbi Shimon says, even the whitewash from a beit haperas from an impure place is pure, for [the Sages] only decreed concerning a clod of earth in its natural state. The dirt of a beit haperas that they smear a roof or an oven with is pure because it is nullified.

A beit haperas (i.e., a field in which a corpse is suspected to be buried), which a dung-heap higher than ten handbreadths was made, and he is able to move it, is pure. [If] its area was made barren, it is impure. Rabban Shimon ben Gamaliel renders it pure. A beit haperas that they paved over with pavement or with stones that cannot be moved is pure. [If] their area was made barren, it is impure. Rabban Shimon ben Gamaliel renders it pure. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says, a beit haperas that they piled up with piles of stones that cannot be moved is impure. Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda says in the name of Rabbi Shimon, [if] they broke the ground [without finding a corpse], there is no better inspection than that. One who walks in a beit haperas lower than three fingerbreadths and removes dirt from there is pure.

One who walks in a beit haperas : He should not walk in another beit haperas , but if he did so walk, he is pure. [If] he harvested grapes in a beit hapares , he should not harvest grapes in another beit hapares , and if he did so harvest, he is impure. These are the words of Beit Hillel.

One who burns consecrated foods and terumah burns them in their place. Rabbi Yehuda says, he burns them outside the Land. And so too would Rabbi Yehuda say, [as to] a field in which a grave was dug up * they may not plant any planting, and they may not sow any seed, and they dig up [the earth] inside it for vegetables, and they may not let [any vegetables] remain inside of it, and they may sprinkle [the waters of purification] and immerse [inside of it] * , and they may not plant cucumbers or gourds inside of it, in order that a man's foot not become accustomed to going there.

A "field in which a grave has been lost" -- it is * a "field of sepulchers" ( sadeh kochin ); a field of sepulchers -- it is a field in which a grave has been lost. * And what is a field of sepulchers? Any that are dug into the earth and the sepulchers are "swallowed up" on their sides. [If] one found a field that was marked off (i.e., indicating that it once was the boundary of an area of impurity), and it is no longer known what the nature [of the impurity] was: If there was a tree in it, it is certain that a grave was plowed up inside it. [If] it does not have a tree in it, it is certain that a grave was lost inside it. Said Rabbi Yehuda, when do these words apply? At a time that there is an elder or a Torah scholar, for not every person is an expert in these matters. Rabbi Yosei says, there is a presumption that bones that have been covered up are those of a human, until it is known [with certainty] that they are from an animal. [If] they are exposed, behold, they are [presumed to be] from an animal, unless it is known [with certainty] that they are from a human. Beit Shammai agrees with Beit Hillel that [a beit haperas ] is not checked for [one who intends to eat] terumah; rather, it is burned.

There is a stringency with the land of the nations that there is not with a beit haperas , and with a beit haperas that there is not with the land of the nations: That with the land of the nations, virgin [soil] that has not been defiled, and then becomes defiled when one enters it, and it cannot be purified from its defilement, which is not the case with a beit haperas . The stringency with a beit haperas is that even if the four sides surrounding it are pure, behold, it still has the presumption of a beit haperas . The land of the nations: If one is able to enter it in a state of purity, it is pure. And how close must one be to be able to enter it in a state of purity? Rabban Shimon ben Gamaliel says, even one furrow, behold, that interrupts. Said Rabbi Shimon, I could feed priests foods prepared in purity in a tannery that is in Tzidon (i.e., north of the Land of Israel), or that is in the towns that are in Lebanon, because they are adjacent to the sea or to the river. They said to him, behold, the idols interrupt. § The presumption of the roads of those who come up from Babylonia: Even though they are absorbed within the land of the nations, they are pure. Rabban Shimon ben Gamaliel says, up until a place that a person can turn to the right and the left without embarrassment. Towns that have been absorbed within the Land of Israel, such as Susita and its neighbors, [and] Ashkelon and its neighbors, even though they are exempt from tithes and from the [laws of] the sabbatical year, they are not considered [part of] the land of the nations.

One who enters the land of the nations in chest or in a cupboard is pure. In a coach, in a wagon, or in a boat, or on a raft, he is impure. One who inserts his head and the majority of his body into the land of the nations is impure. An earthenware vessel that entered the airspace of the land of the nations is impure. Benches and cathedras (a cushioned chair with a back) whose majority entered the land of the nations are impure.

Everyone can convert [an Israelite dwelling] into a "dwelling places of the nations," even a slave, even a maidservant, and even a eunuch, and even a minor of nine years and one day. * An idolater that is married, and a Samaritan that is married, an idolater whose slaves are Samaritans, and a Samaritan whose slaves are idolaters, make a "dwelling place of the nations." Regarding "suspending" the laws of dwelling places of the nations (i.e., in connection with eating terumah and consecrated foods), Rabbi Yosei b'Rabbi Yehuda says, they only burn it. And how long must [a Gentile] stay in [a dwelling] in order that it requires inspection? Aba Yudan a man of Tzidon in the name of Rabbi Eliezer [says], forty days, even if he does not have a wife, and the halacha is according to his words. [If] this one was entering and that one was leaving, and [neither] remained there for forty days, it is pure, and if [one of them] remained there for forty days, it is impure with corpse-impurity. * A [Gentile] watchman: [If] he remains there for forty days [without leaving], it is impure. When he is one that [is permitted] to come and go, even though he remains there forty days, it is pure because he has the presumption of one who watches * . Everyone is trusted to watch [the dwelling], and even a slave, and even a woman, and even a eunuch, and even a minor of nine years and one day.
Sewer-pipes that travel from the land of the nations into the Land of Israel: He makes two * grates for them and he reduces [their circumference] until it is less than a handbreadth.

How do they inspect a dwelling place of the nations (Mishnah Oholot 18:8). An Israelite enters first, and afterwards a priest. Even if they found that [the dwelling place] was inlaid with alabaster or with mosaic (פספס) (see GR"A), it is impure.

A store is not subject to the laws of "dwelling places of the nations" (Mishnah Oholot 18:10). Even if it was destroyed, behold, it is impure and is not [subject to the laws of] dwelling places of the nations. * And a beit haperas outside the Land [of Israel], horse-mangers * , and workshops, and public baths, and a gate-house, and a reservoir, and the open spaces of the courtyard, and fruit-shelters * , and the way stations, and the temporary huts (succot), the field-huts, and the tents, are not subject to the laws of dwelling places of the nations. Armories and wineries [of gentiles]: Rabbi Yehuda renders them impure and Rabbi Yosei renders them pure * . A gate-house and the open spaces of the courtyard: At a time that they are intermingled with dwelling places of the nations, they are impure on account of the laws of dwelling places of the nations. And double-rows of colonnades: Even if they become intermingled with dwelling places of the nations, they are not subject to the laws of dwelling-places of the nations.

And what is the "east of Caesarea" (Mishnah Oholot 18:9)? From opposite its titraphlon * , until opposite its wine press. Yehuda the Baker testified about the northeast * , that it is [considered] pure, and the remainder of all of it is impure on account of [being part of] the land of the nations.

One who travels from Akko to Cheziv in our days: The road is [considered] pure on account of being [part of] the land of the nations, and it is liable in tithes and in [the laws of] the sabbatical year, unless it is known [with certainty] that it is exempt. From the left-hand side to the west of the road is impure on account of being the land of the nations, and exempt from tithes and from [the laws of] the sabbatical year, unless it is known [with certainty] that it is liable, until Cheziv. Rabbi Yishmael b'Rabbi Yosei says in the name of his father, until Laclabi * .

Originally, they would say that the borders [of Ashkelon (MS Vienna)], from Kever HaGadol * until the Negev, and until Tar'in, were impure. And the Sages voted on them (i.e., the borders), and rendered them pure. Rabbi Yehuda ben Yaakov from Beit Guvria, and Yaakov b'Rabbi Yitzchak from Beit Gufnin, testified about Caesarea, that [the Israelites] had always had it in their possession, but that the Sages permitted it, that it no longer be counted [as part of the Land of Israel * ]. Said Rabbi Chanin, that same year was the sabbatical year, and the idolaters went to their circuses, and they left the marketplace full of produce, and the Israelites came and plundered it. Upon their return, they said, "Come, let us go to the Sages, lest they permit pigs to them." Said Rabbi Zerika, on the fifth day of the second Adar, twenty-four elders voted on it and they permitted it, for everyone was entering inside it.

It so happened with Rebbi and Rabbi Yishmael b'Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Eliezer HaKappar (Bar Kappara), that they spent the Sabbath in the store of Pazi * in Lod, and Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair was sitting before them. They said to him, "Ashkelon, what is your (pl.) ruling about it (i.e., whether it is considered a dwelling place of the nations)?" He said to them, "They sell wheat in their basilicas * , and they join * their Pesach offerings in the evening." They said to him, "What is the ruling for one who traveled in it from the land of the nations?" He said to them, "Once he lingers in it forty days." They said to him, "In that case, come (pl.) and we will vote on it, whether to exempt it from tithes or not." Rabbi Yishmael b'Rabbi Yosei did not vote with them. When he removed [himself], he * said, "Rabbi, for what reason are you not voting with us?" He said to him, "Concerning one impurity that I [previously] rendered impure, I [have] rendered it pure. [But] not tithes. I am afraid of the Supreme Sanhedrin, lest they cut off my head!"
